Changes since OpenSSH 4.7: ============================ Security: * Disable execution of ~/.ssh/rc for sessions where a command has been forced by the sshd_config ForceCommand directive. Users who had write access to this file could use it to execute arbitrary commands. This behaviour was documented, but was an unsafe default and an extra hassle for administrators. New features: * Added chroot(2) support for sshd(8), controlled by a new option "ChrootDirectory". Please refer to sshd_config(5) for details, and please use this feature carefully. (bz#177 bz#1352) * Linked sftp-server(8) into sshd(8). The internal sftp server is used when the command "internal-sftp" is specified in a Subsystem or ForceCommand declaration. When used with ChrootDirectory, the internal sftp server requires no special configuration of files inside the chroot environment. Please refer to sshd_config(5) for more information. * Added a "no-user-rc" option for authorized_keys to disable execution of ~/.ssh/rc * Added a protocol extension method "posix-rename@openssh.com" for sftp-server(8) to perform POSIX atomic rename() operations. (bz#1400) * Removed the fixed limit of 100 file handles in sftp-server(8). The server will now dynamically allocate handles up to the number of available file descriptors. (bz#1397) * ssh(8) will now skip generation of SSH protocol 1 ephemeral server keys when in inetd mode and protocol 2 connections are negotiated. This speeds up protocol 2 connections to inetd-mode servers that also allow Protocol 1 (bz#440) * Accept the PermitRootLogin directive in a sshd_config(5) Match block. Allows for, e.g. permitting root only from the local network. * Reworked sftp(1) argument splitting and escaping to be more internally consistent (i.e. between sftp commands) and more consistent with sh(1). Please note that this will change the interpretation of some quoted strings, especially those with embedded backslash escape sequences. (bz#778) * Support "Banner=none" in sshd_config(5) to disable sending of a pre-login banner (e.g. in a Match block). * ssh(1) ProxyCommands are now executed with $SHELL rather than /bin/sh. * ssh(1)'s ConnectTimeout option is now applied to both the TCP connection and the SSH banner exchange (previously it just covered the TCP connection). This allows callers of ssh(1) to better detect and deal with stuck servers that accept a TCP connection but don't progress the protocol, and also makes ConnectTimeout useful for connections via a ProxyCommand. * Many new regression tests, including interop tests against PuTTY's plink. * Support BSM auditing on Mac OS X The following bugs have been fixed in this release: - scp(1) incorrectly reported "stalled" on slow copies. (bz#799) - scp(1) date underflow for timestamps before epoch. (bz#828) - scp(1) and sftp(1) progressmeter type fixes. (bz#842) - SSH2_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED packets did not correctly reset the client keepalive logic, causing disconnections on servers that did not explicitly implement "keepalive@openssh.com". (bz#1307) - ssh(1) used the obsolete SIG DNS RRtype for host keys in DNS, instead of the current standard RRSIG. (bz#1317) - Extract magic buffer size constants in scp(1) to #defines. (bz#1333) - Correctly drain ACKs when a sftp(1) upload write fails midway, avoids a fatal() exit from what should be a recoverable condition. (bz#1354) - Avoid pointer arithmetic and strict aliasing warnings. (bz#1355) - Fixed packet size advertisements. Previously TCP and agent forwarding incorrectly advertised the channel window size as the packet size, causing fatal errors under some conditions. (bz#1360) - Document KbdInteractiveAuthentication in sshd_config(5). (bz#1367) - Fixed sftp(1) file handle leak on download when the local file could not be opened. (bz#1375) - Fixed ssh-keygen(1) selective host key hashing (i.e. "ssh-keygen -HF hostname") to not include any IP address in the data to be hashed. (bz#1376) - Fix clobbering of struct passwd from multiple getpwid calls, resulting in fatal errors inside tilde_expand_filename. (bz#1377) - Fix parsing of port-forwarding specifications to correctly detect errors in either specified port number. (bz#1378) - Fix memory leak in ssh(1) ~ escape commandline handling. (bz#1379) - Make ssh(1) skip listening on the IPv6 wildcard address when a binding address of 0.0.0.0 is used against an old SSH server that does not support the RFC4254 syntax for wildcard bind addresses. (bz#1381) - Remove extra backslashes in the RB_PROTOTYPE macro definition. (bz#1385) - Support ssh(1) RekeyLimits up to the maximum allowed by the protocol: 2**32-1. (bz#1390) - Enable IPV6_V6ONLY socket option on sshd(8) listen socket, as is already done for X11/TCP forwarding sockets. (bz#1392) - Fix FD leak that could hang a ssh(1) connection multiplexing master. (bz#1398) - Improve error messages when hostname resolution fails due to a system error. (bz#1417) - Make ssh(1) -q option documentation consistent with reality. (bz#1427 bz#1429) Portable OpenSSH bugs fixed: - Fixed sshd(8) PAM support not calling pam_session_close(), or failing to call it with root privileges. (bz#926) - Made sshd(8) use configuration-specified SyslogFacility for hosts_access(3) messages for denied connections. (bz#1042) - Implement getgrouplist(3) for AIX, enabling NSS LDAP to work on this platform. (bz#1081) - Fix compilation errors on AIX due to misdefinition of LLONG_MAX. (bz#1347) - Force use of local glob(3) implementation on Mac OS X and FreeBSD, as the platform versions lack features or have unexpected behaviour. (bz#1407) - Reduce stdout/stderr noise from ssh-copy-id. (bz#1431) - Fix activation of OpenSSL engine support when requested in configure. Other changes, new functionality and fixes in this release: * sshd(8) in new installations defaults to SSH Protocol 2 only. Existing installations are unchanged. * The SSH channel window size has been increased, and both ssh(1) sshd(8) now send window updates more aggressively. These improves performance on high-BDP (Bandwidth Delay Product) networks. * ssh(1) and sshd(8) now preserve MAC contexts between packets, which saves 2 hash calls per packet and results in 12-16% speedup for arcfour256/hmac-md5. * A new MAC algorithm has been added, UMAC-64 (RFC4418) as "umac-64@openssh.com". UMAC-64 has been measured to be approximately 20% faster than HMAC-MD5. * A -K flag was added to ssh(1) to set GSSAPIAuthentication=Yes * Failure to establish a ssh(1) TunnelForward is now treated as a fatal error when the ExitOnForwardFailure option is set. * ssh(1) returns a sensible exit status if the control master goes away without passing the full exit status. (bz #1261) * The following bugs have been fixed in this release: - When using a ProxyCommand in ssh(1), set the outgoing hostname with gethostname(2), allowing hostbased authentication to work (bz #616) - Make scp(1) skip FIFOs rather than hanging (bz #856) - Encode non-printing characters in scp(1) filenames. these could cause copies to be aborted with a "protocol error" (bz #891) - Handle SIGINT in sshd(8) privilege separation child process to ensure that wtmp and lastlog records are correctly updated (bz #1196) - Report GSSAPI mechanism in errors, for libraries that support multiple mechanisms (bz #1220) - Improve documentation for ssh-add(1)'s -d option (bz #1224) - Rearrange and tidy GSSAPI code, removing server-only code being linked into the client. (bz #1225) - Delay execution of ssh(1)'s LocalCommand until after all forwadings have been established. (bz #1232) - In scp(1), do not truncate non-regular files (bz #1236) - Improve exit message from ControlMaster clients. (bz #1262) - Prevent sftp-server(8) from reading until it runs out of buffer space, whereupon it would exit with a fatal error. (bz #1286) * Portable OpenSSH bugs fixed: - Fix multiple inclusion of paths.h on AIX 5.1 systems. (bz #1243) - Implement getpeereid for Solaris using getpeerucred. Solaris systems will now refuse ssh-agent(1) and ssh(1) ControlMaster clients from different, non-root users (bz #1287) - Fix compilation warnings by including string.h if found. (bz #1294) - Remove redefinition of _res in getrrsetbyname.c for platforms that already define it. (bz #1299) - Fix spurious "chan_read_failed for istate 3" errors from sshd(8), a side-effect of the "hang on exit" fix introduced in 4.6p1. (bz #1306) - pam_end() was not being called if authentication failed (bz #1322) - Fix SELinux support when SELinux is in permissive mode. Previously sshd(8) was treating SELinux errors as always fatal. (bz #1325) - Ensure that pam_setcred(..., PAM_ESTABLISH_CRED) is called before pam_setcred(..., PAM_REINITIALIZE_CRED), fixing pam_dhkeys. (bz #1339) - Fix privilege separation on QNX - pre-auth only, this platform does not support file descriptor passing needed for post-auth privilege separation. (bz #1343) Thanks to everyone who has contributed patches, reported bugs and tested releases. The signal handler was vulnerable to a race condition that could be exploited to perform a pre-authentication denial of service. On portable OpenSSH, this vulnerability could theoretically lead to pre-authentication remote code execution if GSSAPI authentication is enabled, but the likelihood of successful exploitation appears remote. * On portable OpenSSH, fix a GSSAPI authentication abort that could be used to determine the validity of usernames on some platforms. This release includes the following new functionality and fixes: * Implemented conditional configuration in sshd_config(5) using the "Match" directive. This allows some configuration options to be selectively overridden if specific criteria (based on user, group, hostname and/or address) are met. So far a useful subset of post- authentication options are supported and more are expected to be added in future releases. * Add support for Diffie-Hellman group exchange key agreement with a final hash of SHA256. * Added a "ForceCommand" directive to sshd_config(5). Similar to the command="..." option accepted in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, this forces the execution of the specified command regardless of what the user requested. This is very useful in conjunction with the new "Match" option. * Add a "PermitOpen" directive to sshd_config(5). This mirrors the permitopen="..." authorized_keys option, allowing fine-grained control over the port-forwardings that a user is allowed to establish. * Add optional logging of transactions to sftp-server(8). * ssh(1) will now record port numbers for hosts stored in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys when a non-standard port has been requested. * Add an "ExitOnForwardFailure" option to cause ssh(1) to exit (with a non-zero exit code) when requested port forwardings could not be established. * Extend sshd_config(5) "SubSystem" declarations to allow the specification of command-line arguments. * Replacement of all integer overflow susceptible invocations of malloc(3) and realloc(3) with overflow-checking equivalents. * Many manpage fixes and improvements * New portable OpenSSH-specific features: - Add optional support for SELinux, controlled using the --with-selinux configure option (experimental) - Add optional support for Solaris process contracts, enabled using the --with-solaris-contracts configure option (experimental) This option will also include SMF metadata in Solaris packages built using the "make package" target - Add optional support for OpenSSL hardware accelerators (engines), enabled using the --with-ssl-engine configure option. * Bugs from http://bugzilla.mindrot.org fixed: #482 - readconf doesn't accept paths with spaces in them. #906 - This behaviour has been changed in OpenSSH 4.2 to only delegate credentials to users who authenticate using the GSSAPI method. This eliminates the risk of credentials being inadvertently exposed to an untrusted user/host (though users should not activate GSSAPIDelegateCredentials to begin with when the remote user or host is untrusted) - Added a new compression method that delays the start of zlib compression until the user has been authenticated successfully. The new method ("Compression delayed") is on by default in the server. This eliminates the risk of any zlib vulnerability leading to a compromise of the server from unauthenticated users. NB. Older OpenSSH (<3.5) versions have a bug that will cause them to refuse to connect to any server that does not offer compression when the client has compression requested. Since the new "delayed" server mode isn't supported by these older clients, they will refuse to connect to a new server unless compression is disabled (on the client end) or the original compression method is enabled on the server ("Compression yes" in sshd_config) - Another round of proactive changes for signed vs unsigned integer bugs has been completed, including changing the atomicio() API to encourage safer programming. This work is ongoing. - Added support for the improved arcfour cipher modes from draft-harris-ssh-arcfour-fixes-02. The improves the cipher's resistance to a number of attacks by discarding early keystream output. - Increase the default size of new RSA/DSA keys generated by ssh-keygen from 1024 to 2048 bits. - Many bugfixes and improvements to connection multiplexing, including: - Added ControlMaster=auto/autoask options to support opportunistic multiplexing (see the ssh_config(5) manpage for details). - The client will now gracefully fallback to starting a new TCP connection if it cannot connect to a specified multiplexing control socket - Added %h (target hostname), %p (target port) and %r (remote username) expansion sequences to ControlPath. Also allow ControlPath=none to disable connection multiplexing. - Implemented support for X11 and agent forwarding over multiplexed connections. Because of protocol limitations, the slave connections inherit the master's DISPLAY and SSH_AUTH_SOCK rather than distinctly forwarding their own. - Portable OpenSSH: Added support for long passwords (> 8-char) on UnixWare 7. - The following bugs from http://bugzilla.mindrot.org/ were closed: #471 - Misleading error message if /dev/tty perms wrong #623 - Don't use $HOME in manpages #829 - Don't allocate a tty if -n option is set #1025 - Correctly handle disabled special character in ttymodes #1033 - Fix compile-time warnings #1046 - AIX 5.3 Garbage on Login #1054 - Don't terminate connection on getpeername() failure #1076 - GSSAPIDelegateCredentials issue mentioned above - Lots of other improvements and fixes. Please refer to the ChangeLog for details Thanks to everyone who has contributed patches, problem or test reports. Some notable fixes are: - Fix segfault when using forwardings configured in ssh_config(5) and ClearAllForwardings (bugzilla #996) - Limit input buffer size for channels. A peer could send more data than the buffer code was willing to accept. This would cause OpenSSH to abort the connection (bugzilla #896) * Several improvements to the regression tests * Portable OpenSSH: - OpenSSH will now always normalise IPv4 in IPv6 mapped addresses back to IPv4 addresses. This means that IPv4 addresses in log messages on IPv6 enabled machines will no longer be prefixed by "::ffff:" and AllowUsers, DenyUsers, AllowGroups, DenyGroups will match IPv4-style addresses only for 4-in-6 mapped connections. This ensures a consistent representation of IPv4 addresses regardless of whether or not the machine is IPv6 enabled. * Other bugfixes, including bugzilla #950, #997, #998, #999, #1005, #1006, #1024, and #1038 Changes since OpenSSH 3.9: ============================ * ssh(1) now allows the optional specification of an address to bind to in port forwarding connections (local, remote and dynamic). Please refer to the documentation for the -L and -R options in the ssh(1) manual page and the LocalForward and RemoteForward options in the ssh_config(5) manpage. (Bugzilla #413) * To control remote bindings while retaining backwards compatibility, sshd(8)'s GatewayPorts option has been extended. To allow client specified bind addresses for remote (-R) port forwardings, the server must be configured with "GatewayPorts clientspecified". * ssh(1) and ssh-keyscan(1) now support hashing of host names and addresses added to known_hosts files, controlled by the ssh(1) HashKnownHosts configuration directive. This option improves user privacy by hiding which hosts have been visited. At present this option is off by default, but may be turned on once it receives sufficient testing. * Added options for managing keys in known_hosts files to ssh-keygen(1), including the ability to search for hosts by name, delete hosts by name and convert an unhashed known_hosts file into one with hashed names. These are particularly useful for managing known_hosts files with hashed hostnames. * Improve account and password expiry support in sshd(8). The server will now warn in advance for both account and password expiry. * sshd(8) will now log the source of connections denied by AllowUsers, DenyUsers, AllowGroups and DenyGroups (Bugzilla #909) * Added AddressFamily option to sshd(8) to allow global control over IPv4/IPv6 usage. (Bugzilla #989) * Improved sftp(1) client, including bugfixes and optimisations for the ``ls'' command and command history and editing support using libedit. * Improved the handling of bad data in authorized_keys files, eliminating fatal errors on corrupt or very large keys. (Bugzilla #884) * Improved connection multiplexing support in ssh(1). Several bugs have been fixed and a new "command mode" has been added to allow the control of a running multiplexing master connection, including checking that it is up, determining its PID and asking it to exit. * Have scp(1) and sftp(1) wait for the spawned ssh to exit before they exit themselves. This prevents ssh from being unable to restore terminal modes (not normally a problem on OpenBSD but common with -Portable on POSIX platforms). (Bugzilla #950) * Portable OpenSSH: - Add *EXPERIMENTAL* BSM audit support for Solaris systems (Bugzilla #125) - Enable IPv6 on AIX where possible (see README.platform for details), working around a misfeature of AIX's getnameinfo. (Bugzilla #835) - Teach sshd(8) to write failed login records to btmp for unsuccessful auth attempts. Currently this is only for password, keyboard-interactive and challenge/response authentication methods and only on Linux and HP-UX. - sshd(8) now sends output from failing PAM session modules to the user before exiting, similar to the way /etc/nologin is handled - Store credentials from gssapi-with-mic authentication early enough to be available to PAM session modules when privsep=yes. OpenSSH 3.0 was released on 2001-11-06. It is available from the mirrors listed at https://www.openssh.com/. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0 implementation and includes sftp client and server support. This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below). We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support and encouragement. Important Changes: ================== 1) SSH protocol v2 is now the default protocol version use the 'Protocol' option from ssh(1) and sshd(8) if you need to change this. 2) The files /etc/ssh_known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 are now obsolete, you can use /etc/ssh_known_hosts ~/.ssh/known_hosts ~/.ssh/authorized_keys For backward compatibility ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 will still used for authentication and hostkeys are still read from the known_hosts2. However, those deprecated files are considered 'readonly'. Future releases are likely not to read these files. 3) The CheckMail option in sshd_config is deprecated, as sshd(8) no longer checks for new mail. 4) X11 cookies are now stored in $HOME. New Features: ============= 1) Smartcard support in the ssh client and agent based on work by University of Michigan CITI (http://www.citi.umich.edu/projects/smartcard/). 2) support for Rekeying in protocol version 2 3) improved Kerberos support in protocol v1 (KerbIV and KerbV) 4) backward compatibility with older commercial SSH versions >= 2.0.10 5) getopt(3) is now used by all programs 6) dynamic forwarding (use ssh(1) as your socks server) 7) ClearAllForwardings in ssh(1) 8) ssh(1) now checks the hostkey for localhost (NoHostAuthenticationForLocalhost yes/no). 9) -F option in ssh(1) 10) ssh(1) now has a '-b bindaddress' option 11) scp(1) allows "scp /file localhost:/file" 12) The AuthorizedKeysFile option allows specification of alternative files that contain the public keys that can be used for user authentication (e.g. /etc/ssh_keys/%u, see sshd(8)) 13) extended AllowUsers user@host syntax in sshd(8) 14) improved challenge-response support (especially for systems supporting BSD_AUTH) 15) sshd(8) can specify time args as 1h, 2h30s etc. 16) sshd(8) transmits the correct exit status for remote execution with protocol version 2. 17) ssh-keygen(1) can import private RSA/DSA keys generated with the commercial version 18) ssh-keyscan(1) supports protocol version 2 OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. OpenSSH 2.9.9 fixes a weakness in the key file option handling, including source IP based access control. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0 implementation and includes sftp client and server support. This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below). We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support and encouragement. Security Notes: =============== This release fixes weakness in the source IP based access control for SSH protocol v2 public key authentication: Versions of OpenSSH between 2.5 and 2.9.9 are affected if they use the 'from=' key file option in combination with both RSA and DSA keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2. Depending on the order of the user keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 sshd might fail to apply the source IP based access control restriction (e.g. from="10.0.0.1") to the correct key: If a source IP restricted key (e.g. DSA key) is immediately followed by a key of a different type (e.g. RSA key), then key options for the second key are applied to both keys, which includes 'from='. This means that users can circumvent the system policy and login from disallowed source IP addresses. Important Changes: ================== OpenSSH 2.9.9 might have upgrade issues introduced by the long time between releases, which may affect people in unforeseen ways: 1) The files /etc/ssh_known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/known_hosts2 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 are now obsolete, you can use /etc/ssh_known_hosts ~/.ssh/known_hosts ~/.ssh/authorized_keys For backward compatibility ~/.ssh/authorized_keys2 is still used for authentication and hostkeys are still read from the known_hosts2. However, old files are considered 'readonly'. Future releases are likely to not read these files. 2) The CheckMail option in sshd_config is deprecated, sshd no longer checks for new mail. 3) X11 cookies are stored in $HOME OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH protocol version 1.3, 1.5 and 2.0 implementation and includes sftp client and server support. This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below). Important Changes: ================== WARNING: SSH protocol v2 is now the default protocol version use the 'Protocol' option from ssh(1) and sshd(8) if you want to change this. SSH protocol v2 implementation adds support for: HostbasedAuthentication, similar to RhostsRSA in SSH protocol v1 Rekeying (negotiate new encryption keys for the current SSH session, try ~R in interactive SSH sessions) updated DH group exchange: draft-ietf-secsh-dh-group-exchange-01.txt client option HostKeyAlgorithms server options ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax tty mode passing general: gid swapping in sshd (fixes access to /home/group/user based directory structures) Dan Kaminsky <dankamin@cisco.com> contributed an experimental SOCKS4 proxy to the ssh client (yes, client not the server). Use 'ssh -D 1080 server' if you want to try this out. server option PrintLastLog improvements for scp > 2GB improved ListenAddress option. You can now use ListenAddress host:port improved interoperability (bug detection for older implementations) improved documentation OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. Portable OpenSSH 2.5.2p2 is now available from the mirror sites listed at http://www.openssh.com/portable.html Security related changes: Improved countermeasure against "Passive Analysis of SSH (Secure Shell) Traffic" http://openwall.com/advisories/OW-003-ssh-traffic-analysis.txt The countermeasures introduced in earlier OpenSSH-2.5.x versions caused interoperability problems with some other implementations. Improved countermeasure against "SSH protocol 1.5 session key recovery vulnerability" http://www.core-sdi.com/advisories/ssh1_sessionkey_recovery.htm New options: permitopen authorized_keys option to restrict portforwarding. PreferredAuthentications allows client to specify the order in which authentication methods are tried. Sftp: sftp client supports globbing (get *, put *). Support for sftp protocol v3 (draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-01.txt). Batch file (-b) support for automated transfers Performance: Speedup DH exchange. OpenSSH should now be significantly faster when connecting use SSH protocol 2. Preferred SSH protocol 2 cipher is AES with hmac-md5. AES offers much faster throughput in a well scrutinised cipher. Bugfixes: stderr handling fixes in SSH protocol 2. Improved interoperability. Client: The client no longer asks for the passphrase if the key will not be accepted by the server (SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK) Miscellaneous: scp should now work for files > 2GB ssh-keygen can now generate fingerprints in the "bubble babble" format for exchanging fingerprints with SSH.COM's SSH protocol 2 implementation. Portable version: Better support for the PRNGd[1] entropy collection daemon. The --with-egd-pool configure option has been deprecated in favour of --with-prngd-socket and the new --with-prngd-port options. The latter allows collection of entropy from a localhost socket. configure ensures that scp is in the $PATH set by the server (unless a custom path is specified). -d [1] http://www.aet.tu-cottbus.de/personen/jaenicke/postfix_tls/prngd.html Portable OpenSSH 2.5.1p2 has just been uploaded and will be making its way to the mirror sites (http://www.openssh.com/portable.html)in due course. OpenSSH is a 100% complete SSH 1.3 & 1.5 protocol implementation and a 99% SSH 2 protocol implementation, including sftp client and server support. This release contains many portability bug-fixes (listed in the ChangeLog) as well as several new features (listed below). OpenSSH 2.5.0p1 was skipped because of interoperability issues with ssh-1.2.18 => ssh-1.2.22. We would like to thank the OpenSSH community for their continued support and encouragement. Important Changes: ================== 1) Features added to the implementation of the SSH 2 protocol: * agent forwarding * support for -R forwarding * RSA host and userkeys * extended support for older SSH 2 protocol implementations OpenSSH still lacks support for rekeying, so you have to turn off rekeying if your server tries to force this feature. The next release of OpenSSH will probably support rekeying. 2) Damien Miller contributed an interactive sftp client. The sftp client works for both SSH protocol versions. 3) David Mazieres' ssh-keyscan has been added to the OpenSSH distribution. 4) Now there are three types of keys in OpenSSH: RSA1 is used by the SSH 1 protocol only, RSA and DSA keys are used by the SSH 2 protocol implementation. You can generate RSA keys for use with SSH 2 protocol with: $ ssh-keygen -t rsa -f /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key To use RSA or DSA keys in SSH 2 protocol, simply add the public keys to the .ssh/authorised_keys2 file. IdentityFile2, HostDsaKey and DSAAuthentication are obsolete: You can use multiple IdentityFile and HostKey options instead, e.g HostKey /etc/ssh_host_key HostKey /etc/ssh_host_dsa_key HostKey /etc/ssh_host_rsa_key in /etc/sshd_config The option DSAAuthentication has been replaced by PubkeyAuthentication. Fingerprinting works for all types of keys: $ ssh-keygen -l -f $HOME/.ssh/{authorized_keys,known_hosts}{,2} 5) Important changes in the implementation of SSH 1 protocol: The OpenSSH server does not require a privileged source port for RhostsRsaAuthentication, since it adds no additional security. Interoperation with SSH 1.4 protocol 6) New option HostKeyAlias This option allows the user to record the host key under a different name. This is useful for tunneling over forwarded connections or if you run multiple sshd's on different ports on the same machine. Alternatively you can use the UserKnownHostsFile or UserKnownHostsFile2 options to specify separate host key files for the connection. 7) The ReverseMappingCheck is now optional in sshd_config. If you combine this with the 'sshd -u0' option the server will not do DNS lookups when a client connects. 8) Stricter Hostkey Checking 9) Option Change Summary: a) New or changed: ChallengeResponseAuthentication MACs PubkeyAuthentication HostkeyAlias (Client only) Banner (Server only) ReverseMappingCheck (Server only) PermitRootLogin {yes,without-password,forced-commands-only,no} {Allow,Deny}Groups now support supplementary groups sshd -D for monitoring scripts or inittab ssh -t multiple -t force tty allocation b) Obsolete: DsaAuthentication (use PubkeyAuthentication instead) HostDsaKey (use HostKey) Identityfile2 (use Identityfile or -i) SkeyAuthentication (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication) TisAuthentication (use ChallengeResponseAuthentication) OpenSSH is brought to you by Markus Friedl, Niels Provos, Theo de Raadt, Kevin Steves, Damien Miller and Ben Lindstrom. Portable OpenSSH 2.1.1p1 is available from one of the many mirrors listed at: http://www.openssh.com/portable.html Regards, Damien Miller This is to announce the release of openssh-2.1.0, the first stable release of portable OpenSSH to incorporate support for the SSH2 protocol. The SSH2 protocol offers a number of advantages over the SSH1 protocol including standards compliance (SSH2 is on the IETF standards track[1]), improved security and operation without RSA (which is patented in some countries). The SSH2 support in OpenSSH has been developed by Markus Friedl, with support from the OpenBSD team. This is also the first version of the portable version of OpenSSH to offer built-in entropy collection. This removes the requirement for EGD on systems that lack a /dev/random driver. As a result, OpenSSH-2.1.0 now requires a recent version of OpenSSL[2] to compile (version 0.9.5 or later). NB. The portable version of OpenSSH is currently in the process of merging its webpages with the official OpenBSD project. Please use http://www.openssh.com/ from now on. Report from peter@frontierflying.com - Include /usr/local/include and /usr/local/lib for systems that don't do it themselves - -R/usr/local/lib for Solaris - Fix RSAref detection - Fix IN6_IS_ADDR_V4MAPPED macro 20000311 - Detect RSAref - OpenBSD CVS change [sshd.c] - disallow guessing of root password - More configure fixes - IPv6 workarounds from Hideaki YOSHIFUJI <yoshfuji@ecei.tohoku.ac.jp> 20000309 - OpenBSD CVS updates to v1.2.3 [ssh.h atomicio.c] - int atomicio -> ssize_t (for alpha). ok deraadt@ [auth-rsa.c] - delay MD5 computation until client sends response, free() early, cleanup. [cipher.c] - void* -> unsigned char*, ok niels@ [hostfile.c] - remove unused variable 'len'. fix comments. - remove unused variable [log-client.c log-server.c] - rename a cpp symbol, to avoid param.h collision [packet.c] - missing xfree() - getsockname() requires initialized tolen; andy@guildsoftware.com - use getpeername() in packet_connection_is_on_socket(), fixes sshd -i; from Holger.Trapp@Informatik.TU-Chemnitz.DE [pty.c pty.h] - register cleanup for pty earlier. move code for pty-owner handling to pty.c ok provos@, dugsong@ [readconf.c] - turn off x11-fwd for the client, too. [rsa.c] - PKCS#1 padding [scp.c] - allow '.' in usernames; from jedgar@fxp.org [servconf.c] - typo: ignore_user_known_hosts int->flag; naddy@mips.rhein-neckar.de - sync with sshd_config [ssh-keygen.c] - enable ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/known_hosts, ok deraadt@ [ssh.1] - Change invalid 'CHAT' loglevel to 'VERBOSE' [ssh.c] - suppress AAAA query host when '-4' is used; from shin@nd.net.fujitsu.co.jp - turn off x11-fwd for the client, too. [sshconnect.c] - missing xfree() - retry rresvport_af(), too. from sumikawa@ebina.hitachi.co.jp. - read error vs. "Connection closed by remote host" [sshd.8] - ie. -> i.e., - do not link to a commercial page.. - sync with sshd_config [sshd.c] - no need for poll.h; from bright@wintelcom.net - log with level log() not fatal() if peer behaves badly. - don't panic if client behaves strange. ok deraadt@ - make no-port-forwarding for RSA keys deny both -L and -R style fwding - delay close() of pty until the pty has been chowned back to root - oops, fix comment, too. - missing xfree() - move XAUTHORITY to subdir. ok dugsong@. fixes debian bug #57907, too. (http://cgi.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?archive=no&bug=57907) - register cleanup for pty earlier. move code for pty-owner handling to pty.c ok provos@, dugsong@ - create x11 cookie file - fix pr 1113, fclose() -> pclose(), todo: remote popen() - version 1.2.3 - Cleaned up - Removed warning workaround for Linux and devpts filesystems (no longer required after OpenBSD updates) 20000308 - Configure fix from Hiroshi Takekawa <takekawa@sr3.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp> It gives me no little pleasure to announce the first stable release of the Unix port of OpenSSH. It is available in tar.gz and RPM format from one of the mirrors listed at: http://violet.ibs.com.au/openssh/files/MIRRORS.html This release fixes all known issues and is known to compile and function on (at least) recent releases on Linux, Solaris, HPUX and SCO Unixware. Please review the ChangeLog[1] for details on what has changed since the last release. I am holding off on a wider announcement until the mirrors have updated. Thanks to everyone who assisted with testing, bug reports, success stories and most of all, patches :) Special thanks to the OpenBSD developers for giving us OpenSSH to begin with. item.title: Sshole
item.description:
1980

the first star

back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd, right next to your username. in a file everyone could read.

in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon. nobody's supposed to ever log in as it.

a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today

3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980

Addressgithub.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd

the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself"

1990s

how sshd checks your password

ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9…. the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash

you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it

and if the field is just *? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in

1990s

the fine print

one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash

the single unix spec · crypt() · 1997

Addresspubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/crypt.html

pretty clear.

except a lot of programs never check for NULL. they just compare whatever crypt() gives back with the stored field, hit the NULL, and crash

2012

crypt stops saying NULL

so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password

now guess which character they picked for that

"?"

yep. the star. again.

musl · b3c4cc12 · aug 2012

Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12

"reportedly."

musl · b3c4cc12 · the diff

Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12

"should not happen" gone, NULL gone, "*" in

2012

three weeks later

then musl adds sha512 crypt. the thing is, sha512crypt gets slower the longer the password is, so someone could send one giant password and keep your server busy for a long time. so musl just caps it at 256 bytes and refuses anything longer

musl · 88bf5a8a · aug 29 2012

Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=88bf5a8a

twenty days after the "*" commit btw

musl · crypt_sha512.c @ 88bf5a8a

Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/misc/crypt_sha512.c?id=88bf5a8a

so past 256 bytes crypt fails. and when crypt fails… it says "*".

musl · crypt_sha512.c

Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha512.c

literally in the comment the whole time

2016

sshd borrows bob's salt

CVE-2016-6210. ask sshd about a user that doesn't exist and it says no instantly, cause there's nothing to hash. real users take a few ms longer. so just time it and you know who exists

the fix is kinda funny. no real hash to check? sshd grabs some other account's salt and hashes your password anyway, just to waste the same amount of time. still a no, just a slower no

openssh-commits · jul 2016

Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-July/005428.html

"for invalid users." and also, it turns out, real users with a *.

2019 → 2022

the fix for the fix

2019. turns out alpine's docker images had no root password. at all. CVE-2019-5021. alpine fixes it by locking root with !

but without pam, ! also kills ssh keys. and cloud images log in with keys.

2022. alpine 3.16 switches root to *. still locked, keys work again

alpine aports · fbe926af · shipped in 3.16, 2022

Addressgitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/commit/fbe926af.patch

narrator: it did not.

2016 → 2026

ten quiet years

why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a *.

so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows.

some people got really close though

libc-alpha · debian #714219 · 2013

Addresssourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html

a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*". six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0", and closes the bug. one character away.

musl mailing list · dec 2024

Addressopenwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2

this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*", same limit. nobody says "sshd"

openssh-commits · 30 oct 2026

Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html

a security review fixes pick_salt(). the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it.

nov 2026

how i ran into it

i was messing around with openssh, mostly the boring parts where it talks to libc, like the password code. people don't really look at that stuff, they look at the crypto. so i built sshd every way i could think of (glibc, musl, pam, no pam, shadow, no shadow) and threw like 17,600 weird logins at it. weird hashes, broken accounts, passwords way too long

oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it

every build agreed on every login. except musl without pam. that one said yes to things it shouldn't

item.title: Vivaldi 8.3 for Desktop: make bad ads sad
item.description:
We aren’t part of the Big Tech oligarchy, and our business doesn’t depend on knowing all about you to predict when you are ready to buy a new toothbrush. While most browser companies turn your browsing into data for harvesting, and profiles to sell, Vivaldi gives you a European alternative that respects your privacy. With 8.3, we have given our Ad and Tracker Blocker a major upgrade so you can send the surveillance machinery home empty-handed.

We aren’t against respectful advertising. A contextual ad that matches the page you’re reading, and doesn’t follow you around afterwards, is a fair way for a site to pay its writers. The ads we object to are the ones that track and profile you. They follow you from site to site and remember things about you that you never chose to share. The built-in Ad and Tracker Blocker was created to make those bad ads sad. Rad!

How much advertising you want to block depends on YOU, who you are and what you’re reading. Some people want every tracker and ad long gone, and don’t mind if it causes a site to occasionally misbehave. Others want the sites they use to work perfectly every time. Some want a bit of both, depending on the site.

For this release we have given the Ad and Tracker Blocker an extensive rebuild to handle large filter lists more efficiently. We’ve also given it an updated design and new labels.

The updated Ad and Tracker Blocker gives you four default levels of protection to choose from:

Off: turns the built-in blocker off completely Light: blocks most known trackers and some ads Strong: blocks more trackers and ads, sites may break Aggressive: blocks almost all trackers and ads, sites may break

You can set your default level of blocking from settings or when onboarding to Vivaldi. The level you select from here will be applied to all sites, but in Vivaldi we always give you more. Ad blocking shouldn’t be all or nothing. In Vivaldi, you can decide how much of the web gets through, one site at a time, on every device you use. That’s the kind of control a browser should give the people who use it.

Levels really pay off when you set them per site. Put that dj-set on Youtube on full blast without ads breaking your beat with Aggressive. Keep your bank on Light so every form works as expected. Turn protection down on the small independent site you trust and whose ads you’re happy to see. To set a level for the site you’re on, click the shield icon in the Address Bar. Vivaldi remembers your choice, so each site loads the way you decided.

If you are particularly interested in the topic, we’ve also added the option to create “custom” levels. In these levels you configure everything yourself, giving you full control over which blocklists are used. You can add a custom block list either added from a remote URL or from their file manager.

The new Ad and Tracker Blocker is also available for Vivaldi on Android and iOS today, so your protection looks and works the same way on your laptop, your phone and your tablet.

Expanding our love for vertical tabs

Long before vertical tabs were a talking point in our industry, they were introduced as an option in Vivaldi, and we have continued to improve the workflows for those who prefer to have their tabs on the side. With our 8.0 update this year, we introduced a redesign that really gave the vertical tabbers a sought-after update. With 8.3 we’re stepping it up with two new additions. If you like your Tab Bar stacked the same order as your sandwiches, listen up.

With Expand Tab Bar on Hover, you can keep the vertical Tab Bar slim, with just favicons showing, and give the page as much of your screen as possible until you actually need your tabs. When you’re looking for a tab, move your cursor over the Tab Bar and it smoothly expands to show full titles. Move away and it slides right back. The feature works when the Tab Bar sits on the left or right side of the window.

Pinned tabs on a vertical Tab Bar can now sit side by side in a compact grid at the top, neatly and all in order. Your mail, calendar and project tools stay one click away, and there’s far more room for everything else you have open. This is Vivaldi, so if you instead prefer the “old” way with each pinned tab taking a row, there is obviously a setting (Settings > Tabs > Tab Features > Pinned Tabs > Show Pinned Tabs at Full Width).

If you’re yet to try vertical tabs, this is your sign. If you’re already in love with vertical tabs, you’re welcome.

What else is new in Vivaldi 8.3 Paste and Go, for a whole list of links

Someone sends you a long list of links in an email or a chat, and you want to open every one of them. The desperate times of clicking them one by one are finally over! Copy the whole list, paste it in the Address Field, and Vivaldi opens each URL in its own tab. Research sources, someone’s wishlist, the reading list a colleague shared: all of them open simultaneously in each own tab, ready to stack, tile or work through one by one.

Copy Sanitized Link

Links often carry tracking parameters that tell a site who shared them and where they came from. Copy Sanitized Link strips those out before the link reaches your clipboard, so the person you send it to gets the page and nothing else. It’s an easy habit that keeps a bit more of your browsing to yourself.

Faster Reader Mode

Reader Mode has gotten some tender love and caring for 8.3. It now opens faster and scrolls more smoothly, so you can switch from a busy page to a clean, readable article in a moment and settle in.

Support for Tab Groups API

Vivaldi now supports Chrome’s Tab Groups API for extensions, so extensions built around tab groups can now work in Vivaldi.

This is your browser

We cannot repeat this often enough: Vivaldi is an independent employee-owned European company. That means we don’t answer to advertisers or a VC firm pushing features that benefit them instead of you. We don’t collect data, we just want to make a great browser that helps you explore the web.

Every release we do is built for the people who use Vivaldi. With 8.3 we’re giving you more control over what you see, what follows you, and how your tabs look. As our marketing department said: “this is a really on-brand release”.

If Vivaldi helps you explore more, tell someone about it. Helping a friend, colleague or family member make the switch is one of the best ways to fight for a better web.

Vivaldi 8.3 is ready today!

Vivaldi 8.3 is also out today on mobile. Read what’s new in Vivaldi 8.3 on Android and iOS.

As always, thank you for being part of the Vivaldi community. Together, we’re fighting for a better web, one release at a time.

Changelog

Take a look at the full list of changes from Vivaldi 8.2 to 8.3.

item.title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
item.description:
Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64

Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time.

But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited.

Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it.

Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer.

This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB.

So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question.

Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay.

Audio in the Open Source Libdragon

Similar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon, the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space.

Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this “obsolete” hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay.

What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse.

QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize.

A simple transform codec, something like MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work…

The Ultra Low Complexity Codec

During some late-night “research”, I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare.

Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU. For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill.

So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC).

ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax.

In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it.

The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change:

-7 … -2, 2 … 7 - coefficient value 0 - zero run, run length (1 … 16) follows in the next nibble 1 - long zero run, run length (17 … 288) follows in the next two nibbles -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles

Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C.

Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is.

ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications.

Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then!

ULC on the N64

I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch.

The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU.

Float to 16-bit Fixed Point

Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer.

That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point.

While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving at 3072 bytes:

32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes

Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14).

After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is.

Cramming it into the RSP

Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor.

This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job.

(Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now)

So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL. Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer.

The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP.

The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all.

To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio.

ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects.

The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago.

Addendum

A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. The README states:

[...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image.

~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port

Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos!

item.title: Download your favourite YouTube videos
item.description:
You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos

Signal boosting Laura's post that you should absolutely download and archive the stuff that matters to you. The corporate internet is hostile to art and the things you love do not belong to you unless you claim them for yourself. If you've been around for a while on YouTube, just look at your "liked videos" playlist and see how many of the early ones are no longer available (something you literally have to enable in the playlist settings, it's that endemic).

The tools to do this in a basic way are extremely easy to get hold of, and generally have good defaults. I'm also going to talk a little about my own setup, and why it is the weird way it is, but it's definitely overkill for most setups. yt-dlp or one of it's many wrappers 1 will do most of what you need, and a folder on a bulk storage drive or NAS will be plenty sufficient to make sure you always have access to them.

For me though, I had a particular need - I have unfortunately programmed myself to be almost entirely unable to fall asleep without a Many a True Nerd Let's Play on a low volume.

This comes with a couple of issues.

I need to be able to play it on my TV. It has to integrate into my existing NAS infrastructure. I need to be able to organise hundreds of videos across dozens of playlists. This is a bigger sticking point than it sounds. Adding new ones or placing them can't be a manual job. Again, hundreds of videos.

My NAS media library is built around Jellyfin, which has a concept of Playlists but they're really not intended as a first-order organisational structure. You're expected to take a few tracks from a bunch of existing albums and place them in a playlist separate from the actual Library. No, Jellyfin has a very rigid concept of either Movies, TV Shows > Seasons > Episodes, or Artists > Albums > Songs.

TV Shows is the obvious analogue here, and with some really wild finagling I was able to get a setup together that is good enough to satisfy for now2. My setup looks like this:

Jellyfin

In Jellyfin I have a Library setup in TV Shows mode called YouTube. I've turned off all metadata scrapers and the like, and have it set to prefer file data over file names.

ytdl-sub

This is the only yt-dlp wrapper that allowed me to properly maintain the Playlist structure to any extent, and is entirely based on a series of .yaml files. In it's self-hosted docker-compose form, it comes with a web-app VSCode IDE which is honestly super handy - bridges the tech-comfort gap nicely.

I have a custom genre and list of MATN playlists I want it to collect and set metadata for.

You can also see there I have a handful of Folding Ideas videos set as "Documentaries" - this is more in keeping with how ytdl-sub expects to be used.

The truth is that 99% of youtubers, and 99.9% of viewers, don't particularly need to structure everything as playlists within a channel. Most have a much higher proportion of one-off to series videos that make my MATN structure utterly pointless. As such, ytdl-sub defaults to tagging videos with a Season field organised by Year, but it stores them in folders named for the Playlist. This leads to Jellyfin putting every one of those playlist videos in 2 places within the channel - a Year Series, and a Playlist Series:

I only recently realised how to fix this, which is to assign the Playlist title as the Season Number in my ytdl-sub config file - it seems like it should break, but it doesn't:

I could write a script to go in and fix this for all my existing series, but the issue is that once Jellyfin has Imported a video, I can't get it to update the Season Number without fully reimporting the Library, something I'm not really interested in doing for a terabyte of video. Oh, speaking of storage size...

Tdarr

Tdarr is a service that can automatically run through a library of videos and re-encode it in whatever way you desire - usually to some smaller, more efficient format or codec. I use it to encode everything in my media server to HEVC/H.265 as storage is my main bottleneck - processing power is the tradeoff and I have that in spades.

I'm honestly not going to recommend Tdarr unless you are very comfortable looking at a massively complex and poorly designed UI and making the smart decision to do the minimum. Everyone I know who has used it has come in with grand ambitions of brilliant complex workflows and settled on just using the default one because it works fine.

It has a tendency to break on anything remotely complex, and I had to manually tweak a script so that it wouldn't cry any time there was a data stream, but once it gets going it just chugs along re-encoding gigabyte after gigabyte.

It does seem to cause Jellyfin to lose Thumbnail images for reasons I haven't fully figured out, but it's generally fixable either manually, with a "refresh metadata", or in your media management software of choice.

It saved me about 700GB across my 2TB library, though I probably could have avoided some of that cost by just being more picky about my downloads.

Again, I don't really recommend it! But if you're in a pinch, it will absolutely do the job.

item.title: Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM
item.description:
Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.

Discord is ditching Electron and its new app uses less RAM

Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.

“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”

Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.

It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

item.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
item.description:
"Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens...

I have never felt anything close to that.

I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:

When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern.

Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland).

My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services.

I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German.

The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab.

Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland.

A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.

I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads.

Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account.

Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here.

A fucking asphalt cleaning tractor.

I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here?

The user is into ovens The user is into installing appliances The user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe?

My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years.

An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport.

Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen.

My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children.

HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles.

I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?..

item.title: MCP Explained
item.description:
Model Context Protocol

What is MCP?

An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back.

Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope. MCP defines what goes in it: the methods, capability negotiation, transports and auth

or jump to Tools Â· the spec time machine Â· Break it
